title: Life of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)
description:
A comprehensive study of the life of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), the final Messenger of Allah. This course covers the historical context of pre-Islamic Arabia, the Prophet's birth and early life, the revelation of the Quran, the Meccan and Medinan periods, major events such as the Hijrah and the Battle of Badr, and his final years. Drawing from classical sources including Ibn Hisham's Seerah, Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidaya wan-Nihaya, and Ibn al-Qayyim's Zad al-Ma'ad, this course provides authentic and well-referenced narratives that illuminate the Prophet's character, mission, and legacy.

The Seerah (biography of the Prophet) is not merely a historical account but a source of guidance for Muslims in every era. The Quran itself says: 'Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example for whoever has hope in Allah and the Last Day and remembers Allah often.' (Quran 33:21). Through studying his life, we learn about patience, perseverance, justice, mercy, and the practical implementation of Islamic teachings.

Each lesson connects the Prophet's experiences to contemporary challenges, helping learners understand how his sunnah (way of life) remains relevant today. Whether you are new to Seerah studies or seeking to deepen your knowledge, this course offers a structured and comprehensive journey through the most important biography in human history.
short_description: Comprehensive study of Prophet Muhammad's life from pre-Islamic Arabia to his final years

modules.title: Pre-Islamic Arabia and the Prophet's Early Life
modules.description: Understanding the world into which Prophet Muhammad was born

lessons.title: Pre-Islamic Arabia: The Age of Jahiliyyah
lessons.content:
Before the birth of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), the Arabian Peninsula was characterized by what is known as Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance). This period was marked by idolatry, tribal warfare, social injustice, and the neglect of spiritual values. The Ka'bah, built by Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and his son Isma'il (Ishmael) as a house of monotheistic worship, had been filled with 360 idols. Tribal identity was paramount, and blood feuds could last for generations.

Despite the pervasive darkness of Jahiliyyah, there were remnants of the Abrahamic tradition. The Hanifs (those who inclined toward monotheism) sought the original religion of Ibrahim. Waraqah ibn Nawfal, the cousin of Khadijah, was one such Hanif who recognized the truth when the first revelation came. The social structure also had elements that Islam would later refine and institutionalize, such as the sacred months during which fighting was prohibited.

Understanding pre-Islamic Arabia is essential for appreciating the revolutionary nature of Islam's message. The Quran itself describes this period: 'They follow nothing but conjecture and what their own souls desire, even though there has already come to them guidance from their Lord.' (Quran 53:23). This lesson sets the stage for understanding why the coming of the Prophet was such a transformative event in human history.

lessons.title: The Birth and Lineage of Prophet Muhammad
lessons.content:
Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was born in Makkah in the Year of the Elephant (approximately 570 CE), a year that saw the miraculous defeat of Abraha's army that had come to destroy the Ka'bah. His full lineage traces back to Isma'il ibn Ibrahim, connecting him to the great Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him). His father, Abdullah, died before his birth, and his mother Aminah passed away when he was six years old, making him an orphan from a young age.

The Prophet belonged to the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh tribe, a noble but not wealthy family. His grandfather Abd al-Muttalib took custody of him after his mother's death. According to Ibn Hisham's Seerah, Abd al-Muttalib loved his grandson deeply and recognized something special about him. The Prophet was entrusted to Halimah al-Sa'diyah, aBedouin wet nurse, who later testified that she experienced unprecedented blessings during the years she nursed him.

The Prophet's early orphanhood shaped his character profoundly. He experienced loss, hardship, and the realities of life from a young age. Yet he grew into a person of extraordinary character, known in Makkah as Al-Amin (the Trustworthy) and Al-Sadiq (the Truthful). The Quran addresses his early life: 'Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter? And He found you wandering and gave you guidance. And He found you poor and made you self-sufficient.' (Quran 93:6-8).

lessons.title: The Character of Prophet Muhammad Before Prophethood
lessons.content:
Before receiving revelation, Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was already known for his exceptional character. He worked as a shepherd, an occupation shared by many prophets before him including Musa (Moses) and Dawud (David). This humble profession taught him patience, responsibility, and care for others. He later worked in trade and was employed by Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, a successful businesswoman.

The people of Makkah gave him the titles Al-Amin (the Trustworthy) and Al-Sadiq (the Truthful) because of his impeccable honesty and integrity. Even his enemies trusted him with their valuables. When the Quraysh were rebuilding the Ka'bah and disputed who should place the Black Stone (al-Hajar al-Aswad) in its position, they chose Muhammad as the arbiter. His wise solution—placing the stone on a cloth and having representatives of each clan lift it together before he set it in place with his own hands—demonstrated his wisdom and diplomatic skill.

He was known for his contemplative nature, often retreating to the cave of Hira on Mount Nur to meditate and reflect. His marriage to Khadijah, who was fifteen years his senior and a widow of distinction, was a love story that lasted until her death. Khadijah was the first person to believe in his prophethood and supported him through the most difficult years of persecution. Their marriage demonstrates the Islamic emphasis on character over wealth, and mutual support in faith.

modules.title: The Beginning of Revelation and the Meccan Period
modules.description: From the first revelation to the persecution of early Muslims

lessons.title: The First Revelation in the Cave of Hira
lessons.content:
The revelation of the Quran began in the month of Ramadan, approximately 610 CE, when Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was forty years old. Angel Jibril (Gabriel) descended upon him in the cave of Hira on Mount Nur (the Mountain of Light) near Makkah. The first words revealed were: 'Read! In the name of your Lord who created. Created man from a clinging substance. Read! And your Lord is the Most Generous. Who taught by the pen. Taught man that which he knew not.' (Quran 96:1-5).

The Prophet was terrified by this experience and rushed home to Khadijah, who comforted him and took him to Waraqah ibn Nawfal, a Christian scholar. Waraqah recognized the description of the angel and affirmed that Muhammad had been chosen as a prophet, just as Musa (Moses) had been chosen before. He warned the Prophet that his people would oppose him, as they had opposed previous messengers.

The first revelation is a pivotal moment in human history. It marks the beginning of the final divine message to humanity. The cave of Hira itself symbolizes the importance of reflection and solitude in seeking truth. Today, Mount Nur remains a place of pilgrimage for Muslims who wish to connect with this foundational event in Islamic history.

lessons.title: Secret and Open Preaching
lessons.content:
For the first three years after the initial revelation, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) preached Islam secretly. He invited close friends and family members to the new faith. The first to accept Islam among men was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, the Prophet's closest companion, and among women was Khadijah. Other early converts included Ali ibn Abi Talib (the Prophet's cousin and future son-in-law), Zayd ibn Harithah (the Prophet's freed slave and adopted son), and Uthman ibn Affan.

After the revelation of 'And warn your closest relatives' (Quran 26:214), the Prophet began open preaching. He climbed Mount Safa and called out to the Quraysh, asking them what they would think if he told them that an army was approaching from behind a mountain. When they confirmed they trusted his truthfulness, he declared his message of monotheism and warned them of the Day of Judgment.

The Quraysh's reaction was mixed. Some, like Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib (the Prophet's uncle), eventually accepted Islam. Others, like Abu Jahl, became fierce opponents. The Prophet's approach to dawah (calling to Islam) demonstrates important principles: starting with those closest to you, using wisdom and beautiful preaching, and being patient in the face of opposition. The Quran instructs: 'Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.' (Quran 16:125).

lessons.title: Persecution and the Boycott of Banu Hashim
lessons.content:
As more people accepted Islam, the Quraysh intensified their persecution of the early Muslims. Bilal ibn Rabah, an Abyssinian slave, was tortured by his master Umayyah ibn Khalaf for refusing to renounce his faith. Sumayyah bint Khayyat and her husband Yasir were also martyred after enduring severe torture. These early Muslims demonstrated extraordinary patience and steadfastness in the face of persecution.

In approximately 616 CE, the Quraysh imposed a comprehensive boycott against Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib, the Prophet's clans. For three years, no trade, marriage, or social interaction was permitted with them. They were confined to a valley called Shib Abi Talib, where they endured extreme hardship and famine. Despite this, the faith of the Muslims continued to grow. The Prophet remained steadfast, and his followers endured the boycott with remarkable patience.

This period of persecution teaches modern Muslims about the importance of patience (sabr) in the face of adversity. The Quran promises: 'Allah does not burden a soul beyond that it can bear.' (Quran 2:286). The early Muslims' perseverance through torture, boycott, and social ostracism serves as a powerful example of faith under pressure, relevant to Muslims facing persecution in various parts of the world today.

lessons.title: The Year of Sorrow and the Night Journey
lessons.content:
The Year of Sorrow (Aam al-Huzn) was a devastating period for the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). He lost his beloved wife Khadijah, who had been his greatest supporter for twenty-five years, and his protective uncle Abu Talib. Without Abu Talib's protection, the Quraysh intensified their hostility. The Prophet sought refuge in Ta'if, but the people of that city rejected him and drove him out with stones, an incident that caused his feet to bleed.

In this context of grief and rejection came one of the most miraculous events in Islamic history: the Isra' and Mi'raj (the Night Journey and Ascension). The Quran describes: 'Glory be to the One Who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, to show him of Our signs.' (Quran 17:1). During this journey, the Prophet was taken from Makkah to Jerusalem and then through the seven heavens, where he met previous prophets and was given the command of the five daily prayers.

The Isra' and Mi'raj was a divine comfort for the Prophet during his darkest hour. It also established the connection between Makkah and Jerusalem, and elevated the status of al-Masjid al-Aqsa. For Muslims today, this event serves as a reminder that relief comes after hardship, and that the most difficult trials are often followed by the greatest blessings. The Prophet's experience teaches us that even prophets face profound sorrow, and that faith in Allah's plan is the source of strength.

modules.title: The Hijrah and the Medinan Period
modules.description: Migration to Madinah and the establishment of the Muslim community

lessons.title: The Hijrah: Migration to Madinah
lessons.content:
The Hijrah (migration) of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) from Makkah to Madinah in 622 CE is one of the most significant events in Islamic history. It marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar and represents the transition from a persecuted minority to an established community. The Quran describes the Muhajirun (emigrants): 'And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins. And who can forgive sins except Allah? And they do not persist in what they had done while they knew.' (Quran 3:135).

The Prophet's journey was fraught with danger. The Quraysh plotted to assassinate him, but Ali ibn Abi Talib slept in the Prophet's bed to create a diversion. The Prophet and Abu Bakr took refuge in the cave of Thawr, where a spider spun its web over the entrance and a pigeon laid eggs, leading the pursuers to believe no one had entered. This miraculous protection demonstrates Allah's care for His messengers.

In Madinah, the Prophet established the first Muslim community based on the principles of brotherhood (mu'akhah) between the Muhajirun and the Ansar (helpers of Madinah). He drafted the Constitution of Madinah (Sahifat al-Madinah), which established rights and responsibilities for Muslims, Jews, and other communities. This document is considered one of the earliest examples of a pluralistic social contract and demonstrates Islam's emphasis on justice, coexistence, and community building.

lessons.title: The Battle of Badr
lessons.content:
The Battle of Badr, fought on 17 Ramadan 2 AH (624 CE), was the first major military engagement between the Muslims and the Quraysh. Despite being vastly outnumbered—approximately 313 Muslims against over 1,000 Qurayshi fighters—the Muslims achieved a decisive victory. This battle is mentioned in the Quran: 'And already had Allah given you victory at Badr, when you were few in number. Then fear Allah; perhaps you will be grateful.' (Quran 3:123).

The battle demonstrated the Prophet's military acumen and the power of faith over material advantage. Before the battle, the Prophet supplicated: 'O Allah, if this small band perishes today, You will not be worshipped on earth again.' His companions Abu Bakr and Umar each made similar supplications, and it is said that Allah responded: 'I will help you and make you firm.' The Muslims' victory was a turning point that boosted their morale and established them as a force to be reckoned with.

The lessons of Badr extend far beyond the battlefield. It teaches that numerical superiority and material wealth are not the only determinants of success. When a cause is just and its supporters put their trust in Allah, victory is possible against overwhelming odds. This lesson is relevant for Muslims facing challenges in every era, whether in personal struggles, community building, or defending their rights. The Prophet's conduct during the battle—showing mercy to prisoners and distributing spoils fairly—also set standards for ethical conduct in conflict.

lessons.title: The Battle of Uhud and the Battle of the Trench
lessons.content:
The Battle of Uhud (3 AH/625 CE) was a painful lesson for the Muslim community. Despite initial success, the Muslims suffered a setback when the archers disobeyed the Prophet's command to hold their position. The Quran addresses this incident: 'And Allah had certainly favored the believers at Badr when you were few in number. Then fear Allah; perhaps you will be grateful. Remember when you said to the believers, 'Is it not enough for you that your Lord should reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?' Indeed, but if you are patient and fear Allah... your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels.' (Quran 3:124-126).

The battle of Uhud teaches the importance of discipline, obedience to leadership, and not letting worldly desires (in this case, the desire to collect war spoils) interfere with a collective mission. The Prophet himself was injured during this battle, and his uncle Hamza was martyred. Yet the Prophet's conduct—forgiving those who had wavered, burying the martyrs with honor, and maintaining the community—demonstrated his extraordinary character.

The Battle of the Trench (Khandaq, 5 AH/627 CE) saw the Muslims face a confederation of Quraysh and their allies who besieged Madinah for weeks. Salman al-Farisi suggested digging a trench around the city, a tactic unknown in Arabia at the time. During the siege, the Prophet's patience was tested severely, yet he remained steadfast in prayer and trust in Allah. The eventual lifting of the siege through Allah's intervention and internal discord among the enemy is a powerful lesson in patience and divine support. The Quran says: 'Allah sent down His tranquility upon the believers and supported them with angels unseen.' (Quran 9:40).

lessons.title: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah and the Conquest of Makkah
lessons.content:
The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (6 AH/628 CE) is considered by scholars as a victory despite its seemingly unfavorable terms. The Muslims wished to perform Umrah (lesser pilgrimage) but were blocked by the Quraysh. The treaty stipulated a ten-year truce, the return of any Qurayshi who fled to Madinah without the Prophet's permission, and that the Muslims would postpone their pilgrimage that year. The companions were initially disappointed, but Allah revealed: 'Indeed, We have granted you a clear conquest. That Allah may forgive you your sins, the former and the latter, and complete His favor upon you and guide you to a straight path.' (Quran 48:1-2).

The treaty proved to be strategically brilliant. During its term, many Qurayshi leaders witnessed Muslim life and converted to Islam. The message of Islam spread peacefully throughout Arabia. When the Quraysh violated the treaty, the Prophet marched to Makkah with ten thousand followers and conquered it virtually bloodlessly. He entered Makkah saying: 'There is no god but Allah alone, He has no partner. He fulfilled His promise, helped His servant, and honored the army.' He forgave the people of Makkah who had persecuted him and his followers for over two decades.

The Conquest of Makkah is a masterclass in forgiveness and magnanimity. The Prophet's declaration of general amnesty—even for those who had killed his companions—demonstrates the Islamic principle of mercy over revenge. He asked the Quraysh: 'What do you think I will do with you?' They replied: 'You are a generous brother, the son of a generous brother.' He declared: 'Go, for you are free.' This act of forgiveness won hearts and led to the widespread acceptance of Islam across Arabia.

modules.title: The Prophet's Character and Teachings
modules.description: Understanding the sunnah and character of Prophet Muhammad

lessons.title: The Character of the Prophet
lessons.content:
Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) embodied the teachings of the Quran in his daily life. His wife Aisha was asked about his character, and she replied: 'His character was the Quran.' (Sahih Muslim). He was gentle, humble, and compassionate with everyone around him. He would sit with the poor, eat with servants, and treat everyone with dignity regardless of their social status.

The Prophet's humility is evident in numerous hadiths. He would mend his own shoes, patch his own clothes, and milk his own goat. When a Bedouin urinated in the mosque, the companions rushed to stop him, but the Prophet restrained them and gently cleaned the area himself, then spoke to the man kindly about mosque etiquette. He said: 'I have been sent to perfect noble character.' (Sahih al-Bukhari).

His compassion extended to all creation. He instructed: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him be generous to his neighbor. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him be generous to his guest.' (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). These teachings on character form the foundation of Islamic ethics and provide a comprehensive guide for how Muslims should interact with others in their daily lives.

lessons.title: The Prophet's Worship and Devotion
lessons.content:
The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was the most devoted worshipper of Allah. His night prayers (Qiyam al-Layl) were so consistent that his feet would swell. When Aisha asked him why he worshipped so much when Allah had forgiven his past and future sins, he replied: 'Should I not be a grateful servant?' (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). His devotion was not merely ritual but encompassed every aspect of his life.

The Prophet would pray the optional forenoon prayers (Duha) and the late-night prayers (Tahajjud) regularly. He would recite long portions of the Quran in prayer, sometimes completing a juz' (one-thirtieth of the Quran) in a single rak'ah. His recitation was characterized by tears and deep reflection. He said: 'The one who is proficient with the Quran will be with the noble, righteous scribes (angels), and the one who recites it and finds it difficult, stumbling through it, will have a double reward.' (Sahih al-Bukhari).

His devotion also extended to dhikr (remembrance of Allah). He would say SubhanAllah (Glory be to Allah) 33 times, Alhamdulillah (All praise is due to Allah) 33 times, and Allahu Akbar (Allah is the Greatest) 33 times after every prayer. He taught that 'the best remembrance is La ilaha illallah (There is no god but Allah).' These practices form the foundation of Islamic spiritual life and provide a blueprint for Muslims seeking to develop a deeper connection with Allah.

lessons.title: The Prophet as a Leader and Decision-Maker
lessons.content:
Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) demonstrated exceptional leadership qualities that are studied and admired even by non-Muslim scholars. His leadership was characterized by consultation (shura), justice, compassion, and strategic thinking. Before major decisions, he would consult his companions, as the Quran commands: 'And those who have responded to their Lord and established prayer and whose affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves.' (Quran 42:38).

A remarkable example of his consultative leadership occurred before the Battle of Badr. While the Muslims were camped near Badr, the Prophet held a council of war and asked his companions for their opinions. Abu Bakr spoke, then Umar, and then the young Ali ibn Abi Talib, whose advice the Prophet accepted. This demonstrates that in Islamic leadership, wisdom is valued over seniority.

The Prophet's leadership also involved empowering others. He appointed governors, judges, and military commanders based on merit. He delegated authority and trusted his companions to carry out important missions. Mu'adh ibn Jabal was sent to Yemen as a judge and teacher, and the Prophet advised him: 'You will encounter people of the Book, so let the first thing you invite them to be the testimony that there is no god but Allah. If they obey you in that, then inform them that Allah has obligated upon them five prayers in every day and night. If they obey you in that, then inform them that Allah has obligated upon them charity (zakat) from their wealthy to be taken from their poor.' (Sahih al-Bukhari). This hadith outlines a comprehensive approach to leadership and community development.

modules.title: The Final Years and Legacy
modules.description: The Prophet's farewell, his passing, and his enduring legacy

lessons.title: The Farewell Pilgrimage and Sermon
lessons.content:
In 10 AH (632 CE), the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) performed his only Hajj, known as the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada'). During this pilgrimage, he delivered one of the most famous speeches in human history at the Plain of Arafat. In his sermon, he declared: 'O people, your Lord is One and your father Adam is one. An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor does a non-Arab have superiority over an Arab; a white person has no superiority over a black person, nor does a black person have superiority over a white person, except by piety and good action.'

He reminded the people of the sanctity of life, property, and honor: 'Your blood, your property, and your honor are sacred to one another, like the sanctity of this day, in this month, in this city.' He emphasized the rights of women, the importance of fulfilling trusts, and the prohibition of usury (riba). He asked: 'Have I conveyed the message?' The people responded: 'Yes!' He raised his hands and said: 'O Allah, bear witness.'

This sermon encapsulates the core values of Islam: equality, justice, the sanctity of life, and accountability before Allah. It is remarkable for its time, declaring universal human dignity centuries before such concepts were recognized in international law. The Prophet's emphasis on the rights of women, the prohibition of exploitation, and the brotherhood of humanity continues to guide Muslims in building just and compassionate societies.

lessons.title: The Prophet's Final Days and Passing
lessons.content:
In the final days of his life, Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) fell ill with a fever that would prove to be his last. Despite his illness, he continued to lead the prayers and attend to the affairs of the community. He instructed Abu Bakr to lead the prayers in his absence, a decision that showed his foresight in establishing clear succession.

During his final illness, the Prophet's concern was for his ummah (community). He said: 'There should be no double riba (usury) and no revenge in matters of religion (i.e., after the conquest of Makkah). Beware of Allah regarding the rights of women. You have rights over your wives and your wives have rights over you.' He also said: 'Take care of the prayer and what your right hands possess (slaves). Allah will guide you.' These final instructions demonstrate his lifelong commitment to the welfare of his followers.

The Prophet passed away on Monday, 12 Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH (632 CE), in the house of Aisha, with his head in her lap. He was approximately 63 years old. His passing was a moment of profound grief for the Muslim community. Umar ibn al-Khattab, in his shock and denial, declared: 'He has not died; he has gone to his Lord as Musa went.' But Abu Bakr reminded the people: 'Whoever worshipped Muhammad, let him know that Muhammad has died. And whoever worshipped Allah, let him know that Allah is alive and never dies.' (Sahih al-Bukhari). The Prophet was buried in the room of Aisha, which later became part of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah.

lessons.title: The Prophet's Legacy and Modern Relevance
lessons.content:
The legacy of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) extends far beyond his physical life. His teachings, preserved in the Quran and the Sunnah, have guided billions of Muslims for over 1,400 years. His example encompasses every aspect of life—worship, family, business, governance, and social interaction. The Quran testifies: 'We have not sent you except as a mercy to all the worlds.' (Quran 21:107).

The Prophet's legacy is evident in numerous areas. His emphasis on knowledge led to the Islamic Golden Age, when Muslim scholars made groundbreaking contributions to science, mathematics, medicine, philosophy, and literature. His principles of justice influenced the development of international law and human rights. His teachings on charity and economic justice provided the foundation for Islamic finance and social welfare systems.

For modern Muslims, the Prophet's life offers practical guidance for contemporary challenges. His patience in the face of persecution teaches resilience. His forgiveness of enemies demonstrates the power of mercy over revenge. His consultation with companions models participatory leadership. His treatment of women, slaves, and non-Muslims illustrates Islamic principles of justice and human dignity. The Prophet said: 'I have left among you two things that if you hold fast to them, you will never go astray: the Book of Allah and my Sunnah.' (Sahih al-Muwatta'). His life remains the ultimate guide for Muslims seeking to live in accordance with Allah's will in the modern world.
